text: Nerve excitability is increased by:
textbookEdition: INT 102 — Introduction to Biomedical Sciences, Academic Year 2026-2027 (Faculty of Medicine, Cairo University)
evidence: Electrolyte effects on nerve excitability are not discussed in this book. By outside physiology: hyperkalemia partially depolarizes the resting membrane potential toward threshold and so increases excitability (at very high levels it eventually blocks conduction, but 'increased excitability' is the classic teaching point for the options given); hypokalemia and hypercalcemia both reduce excitability, and hyponatremia mainly reduces action-potential amplitude rather than increasing excitability.

evidence: Nerve conduction properties are not discussed in this book. By outside physiology: the region immediately behind a travelling impulse is refractory (ensuring one-way propagation); conduction velocity is directly, not inversely, related to fibre diameter; propagation along a myelinated fibre jumps node-to-node within the same neuron, not between neurons; and a true action potential is non-decremental (constant amplitude), unlike the local response.

reviewNote: Question 14 (polycythemia). The book confirms that primary polycythemia (polycythemia vera) is usually accompanied by increased WBC and platelet production, that it increases blood viscosity, and that secondary polycythemia occurs at high altitude — so options A, B and C are all true per the text, leaving D (“can result from excessive secretion of erythropoietin hormone”) as the best-supported exception by elimination. However, D is also a defensible TRUE statement in general medicine, since secondary polycythemia can genuinely result from an EPO-secreting tumor (e.g. renal cell carcinoma) or from exogenous EPO — the book simply does not frame secondary polycythemia in EPO terms. This creates a real risk that more than one option is defensible as the intended “except,” depending on whether “polycythemia” in the stem is read as polycythemia vera specifically (EPO-independent, favouring D as the exception) or polycythemia in general (where D would actually be true). Faculty should confirm the intended scope of the question before this is auto-scored.

evidence: The book describes genuinely opposite, symmetric actions on intestinal smooth muscle: sympathetic causes "Relaxation of the plain muscles of the wall... and Contraction of the sphincters" (p.174), while parasympathetic (vagal) causes "Contraction of plain muscles of the wall... and Relaxation of the sphincters" (p.177) — an explicit, textbook-stated opposite-effects pair. text: Which of the following is a ganglion stimulant?
textbookEdition: INT 102 — Introduction to Biomedical Sciences, Academic Year 2026-2027 (Faculty of Medicine, Cairo University)
evidence: The book defines nicotinic receptors (activated by nicotine) at autonomic ganglia (p.180) and states "Ganglion stimulants: stimulate nicotinic receptors for both sympathetic and parasympathetic ganglia" (p.184), supporting nicotine as a ganglion stimulant; none of the other options (muscarine, atropine, anticholinesterase) acts on nicotinic/ganglionic receptors specifically.
reviewNote: Classic pharmacology describes nicotine’s action on ganglia as dose-dependent/biphasic: small doses stimulate, while persistently high ("large") doses cause depolarizing ganglionic blockade rather than stimulation. The book does not address this dose-dependence, and the option’s specific wording ("large dose") is in tension with that well-known biphasic effect, even though nicotine remains the only nicotinic-receptor agonist among the four options.

text: Regarding caffeine, which of the following is correct?

options.text: It is a central nervous system inhibitor
Its catabolism doesn't produce uric acid in the body
It is contraindicated to take it in diet in case of gout

textbookEdition: INT 102 — Introduction to Biomedical Sciences, Academic Year 2026-2027 (Faculty of Medicine, Cairo University)
evidence: The book does not mention caffeine anywhere. Biochemically, methylxanthines such as caffeine are metabolized mainly by demethylation and are poor substrates for xanthine oxidase (the enzyme that converts purines to uric acid), so their catabolism does not meaningfully raise uric acid production — consistent with option c and with clinical/epidemiological evidence that coffee/caffeine intake is not associated with increased gout risk (if anything, some studies show an inverse association).
reviewNote: This is independent reasoning outside the book, and the two "correct-sounding" options (c and d) are mutually exclusive: if caffeine catabolism truly does not produce uric acid, there is little biochemical basis for singling it out as contraindicated in gout (option d). Different sources and teaching traditions disagree on this point, so a faculty decision is appropriate before scoring.
